prompt: A phone on a café's Wi-Fi shows full bars, and Tickets cannot load the list. What does that show?
hint: What does "connected" promise?

choices.text: Tickets's timeouts are set wrong
choices.why: Any timeout fails when nothing passes; the network is the cause here.

choices.text: Connected means a link, not answers
choices.why: Right. The café passes nothing until its terms are accepted, while the bars stay full.

choices.text: Android is reporting the signal wrongly
choices.why: The signal is strong; what is missing is anything passing through it.

choices.text: The café lets browsers through and blocks every app on purpose
choices.why: Until the terms are accepted the café passes nothing, to browsers or apps.

prompt: Match each property of a poor connection to what it does to a request.
hint: The table of section 02.

pairs.right: a large answer arrives slowly, in pieces
pieces sent again, or an answer that never comes
open connections break when the address changes

prompt: On the same bad network one request is a slow success and another a failure. What decides which?
hint: Section 02, where the failure is decided.

choices.text: The status code the server sends
choices.why: In both cases the server may have answered 200; the client may never see it.

choices.text: Whether Android reports the network as connected
choices.why: Android can report a connection that delivers nothing in time.

choices.text: The client's timeouts
choices.why: Right. Its connect and read limits turn slow into failed.

choices.text: The number of bytes in the answer
choices.why: Size matters to how long it takes; the limit decides what counts as too long.

prompt: By the table of section 02, at least how many round trips does a new HTTPS connection need before the first byte of the answer?
hint: TCP's handshake, TLS's, and the request.

prompt: Why does slow-proxy.mjs draw its drops from a seeded generator instead of Math.random()?
hint: What happens on the second run?

choices.text: Math.random() is too slow for a server
choices.why: Speed is not the issue; repeatability is.

choices.text: So that one SEED loses the same answers every run
choices.why: Right. A failure seen once can then be shown again, and fixed.

choices.text: Math.random() rarely gives numbers below 0.5
choices.why: It is uniform; the seed is about getting the same numbers again.

choices.text: Node has no Math.random() outside a browser
choices.why: It has; it simply cannot be seeded.

prompt: The proxy sends every request on and spoils only the answer. Why is that the case most worth testing?
hint: Who knows what happened when an answer is lost?

choices.text: A lost request would crash boxoffice
choices.why: A request that never arrives does nothing to the server at all.

choices.text: Requests are small, so networks do not lose them
choices.why: Any message can be lost; the point is which loss does harm unseen.

choices.text: A proxy has no way to hold a request
choices.why: It could hold one as easily as an answer; the choice is deliberate.

choices.text: The server acted, and the client cannot know it
choices.why: Right. To the client it looks like a request that never left, and it is the worse case.

prompt: In the run with DROP=0.3, how many of the ten answers did the proxy drop?
hint: Count the 000s, or the proxy's log.

prompt: Through DELAY=6000, curl --max-time 5 ends with exit 28. What does that show?
hint: How long did boxoffice itself take?

choices.text: That boxoffice took six seconds to answer
choices.why: boxoffice answered in milliseconds; the proxy held the answer.

choices.text: Too slow looks the same as no network
choices.why: Right. To curl, six seconds of silence and a dead link end the same way.

choices.text: That the proxy dropped the answer
choices.why: DROP was 0; the answer was held, not thrown away.

choices.text: That code 28 means the connection was refused
choices.why: 28 is curl's timeout; a refusal is 7.

prompt: With -w '%{http_code}', curl prints ___ for a request that received no status at all.
hint: Three digits.

prompt: After the three tries without a key, sh-103 has one seat left of four. Why?
hint: Read the proxy's log of the same kind of run.

choices.text: curl sent each of its requests three times
choices.why: Each curl sent one request; there were three tries in all.

choices.text: Each lost answer was an order boxoffice made
choices.why: Right. Three orders, and the client heard about one.

choices.text: The proxy placed orders of its own
choices.why: The proxy only forwards; boxoffice made every order.

choices.text: The seat count lags behind, like the sales report
choices.why: seats_left is computed at once; only the report lags.

prompt: In the run with the key, the third try came back 201 with idempotent-replayed true. Which order is it?
hint: When was the order actually made?

choices.text: A new order the third try made
choices.why: A new order would not be marked as replayed.

choices.text: A copy the proxy kept from the first answer
choices.why: The proxy keeps nothing; boxoffice replayed it.

choices.text: The first try's, replayed
choices.why: Right. Same key, same body: boxoffice answered with the order the first try made.

choices.text: An order boxoffice retried by itself
choices.why: boxoffice does not retry; the client did, with the same key.

prompt: Why does poor-network.test.mjs read seats_left from BASE and not through LINK?
hint: What could happen to the check itself on the lossy link?

choices.text: LINK does not forward GET requests
choices.why: It forwards every method; that is not the reason.

choices.text: A check through the link could be lost and fail for the wrong reason
choices.why: Right. The assertion that matters is made where nothing can drop it.

choices.text: BASE answers faster
choices.why: Speed is not the point; the link is not slow here, only lossy.

choices.text: The proxy rewrites JSON bodies
choices.why: It passes the body as boxoffice sent it.

prompt: With the payment proxy at DELAY=2500, the second order is a 504. What happened at the payment stub?
hint: The stub's log and its list of requests.

choices.text: It never received the second charge
choices.why: The proxy sends every request on at once; the stub has both charges.

choices.text: It answered slowly, past two seconds
choices.why: It answered at once; the proxy held its answer.

choices.text: It declined the charge
choices.why: It approved both; its log says 201 approve twice.

choices.text: It approved a failed order
choices.why: Right. A customer charged for an order the app reports as failed.

prompt: After the 201 and the 504 through the payment proxy, how many seats does sh-103 have left?
hint: A failed order does not hold its seats.

prompt: Tickets has a saved copy and boxoffice answers through a proxy that holds answers for six seconds. What does the list screen show after Refresh?
hint: Line 56, then line 64.

choices.text: The fresh list, six seconds later
choices.why: The read limit is five seconds of silence, so the answer never arrives in time.

choices.text: The saved copy and the Offline banner
choices.why: Right. The read times out, and the catch shows the copy with its time.

choices.text: The error line, although a copy exists
choices.why: The error line is for no copy at all; line 64 uses the copy.

choices.text: A progress indicator, then the list
choices.why: Tickets has no indicator; section 05 lists that as a question for a test.

prompt: Why does SlowNetworkTest use two proxies, one holding answers for six seconds and one for three?
hint: Tickets waits five.

choices.text: To pin the timeout from both sides
choices.why: Right. Raise it past six and the first fails; lower it under three and the second does.

choices.text: Because Espresso needs one server per test class
choices.why: One server could serve both tests; the two delays are the point.

choices.text: One for the list screen and one for the show's screen
choices.why: Both tests are on the list screen; only the delay differs.

choices.text: The emulator reaches one port of the computer per proxy
choices.why: It reaches any port at 10.0.2.2; the reason is the timeout.

prompt: Which option starts lesson 14's emulator with the delay of a GPRS network?
hint: The help text lists two options.

choices.text: -netspeed gprs
choices.why: That sets the bandwidth of GPRS, not its delay.

choices.text: -netdelay gprs
choices.why: Right. Between 35 and 200 ms, by the emulator's table.

choices.text: adb shell svc data disable
choices.why: That removes mobile data altogether.

choices.text: adb emu network speed gsm
choices.why: That changes the speed of an emulator already running.

prompt: Which of these take the network away from the emulator, or slow it down?
hint: Section 05's two lists of commands.

choices.text: adb shell svc wifi disable
choices.why: Right. Wi-Fi off, mobile data untouched.

choices.text: adb shell cmd connectivity airplane-mode enable
choices.why: Right. Every radio at once.

choices.text: adb emu network speed edge
choices.why: Right. The console of a running emulator, at EDGE's speed.

choices.text: adb shell am force-stop example.tickets
choices.why: That stops the app (lesson 21); the network stays as it was.

choices.text: adb shell input keyevent KEYCODE_HOME
choices.why: That sends the app to the background; the network is untouched.

prompt: A test orders through a proxy with DROP=0.5 and a random seed, retrying with one key. What should it assert?
hint: What holds whichever answers are lost?

choices.text: That the first answer is a 201
choices.why: With a random seed the first answer may be the one lost.

choices.text: That exactly two answers were lost
choices.why: How many are lost changes with the seed.

choices.text: That one seat was taken
choices.why: Right. The seat count holds whatever the network did.

choices.text: That the whole order took less than 100 milliseconds
choices.why: A duration is a window to assert loosely, and it is not what this test is about.

prompt: Tickets shows the Offline banner, and then the network comes back. What brings the fresh list?
hint: Section 06, when the network comes back.

choices.text: Nothing: Tickets notices and reloads by itself
choices.why: Nothing in its code refreshes on its own.

choices.text: Pressing Refresh
choices.why: Right. display hides the banner first, so a fresh load leaves none.

choices.text: Tapping the banner to dismiss it
choices.why: The banner has no tap handler; it is a TextView.

choices.text: Turning the phone, which reloads the list
choices.why: A rotation does reload, by recreating the activity; that is a side effect, not the way back.

prompt: Put the steps of anAnswerSlowerThanTheTimeoutShowsTheSavedCopy in the order they happen.
hint: A copy has to be saved before the slow network can show it.
items: The first load reaches boxoffice directly and saves a copy
Shows.baseUrl is moved behind the six-second proxy
Five seconds pass with no data
The catch shows the saved copy

prompt: A developer raises Tickets's readTimeout from 5000 to 10000. Which test of SlowNetworkTest fails?
hint: Which proxy is now inside the limit?

choices.text: aSlowAnswerInTimeIsShownFresh
choices.why: Three seconds was inside five and is still inside ten; it passes.

choices.text: Both of them
choices.why: Only one of the two delays changes sides of the limit.

choices.text: Neither: they do not read the timeout
choices.why: They do not read it; they are built on either side of it.

choices.text: anAnswerSlowerThanTheTimeoutShowsTheSavedCopy
choices.why: Right. Six seconds is now in time, so the list is fresh and the banner never appears.

prompt: A shopping app retries POST /v1/orders after a timeout, without an Idempotency-Key. boxoffice logs three POST 201s; the customer saw one confirmation. What do you report?
hint: Who made the second and third request, and with what?

choices.text: A boxoffice defect: it should refuse a second identical POST
choices.why: Without a key, two identical bodies are two purchases, as a person may buy twice on purpose.

choices.text: A client defect: it retries a purchase with no key
choices.why: Right. Section 04 showed every lost answer becoming an order.

choices.text: A network defect, for the operator to fix
choices.why: Lost answers are an ordinary day on a phone; the client has to cope.

choices.text: No defect: the customer received a confirmation
choices.why: Three seats were taken and three orders made for one confirmation.
